source_text: XXII. Haec est Doctrina Bellarmini libri jam citati capite septimo. Ubi Respondens ad septimam objectionem affirmat, hominem in puris naturalibus conditum futurum fuisse quales nos sumus, quoad corporis mortalitatem, rebellionem membrorum, ignorantiam, difficultatem & similia. Et postea in solutione Objectionis octavae negat naturalem carnis nostrae impetum magis nunc esse rebellem, quam ante sine gratia futurus erat: & pura naturalia saniora futura fuisse ante peccatum, quam modo sint post peccatum. Adeoque in sequentibus concedit, hominem condi potuisse in tali purae naturae statu, ut in eo esset praeceps ad vitia inclinatio, & impetus sensualitatis. Et pertendit nihil absurdi sequuturum esse, si homini sic in puris naturalibus condito Deus negaret gratiam quae malis ejusmodi medetur, & homini necessaria est, ut ad beatitudinem aeternam perveniat.
english: This is Bellarmine's teaching in chapter 7 of the book already cited. Answering the seventh objection there, he says that man created in a purely natural state would have been just as we are with respect to bodily mortality, the rebellion of the members, ignorance, difficulty and the like.

Later, answering the eighth objection, he denies that the natural drive of our flesh is more rebellious now than it would have been earlier without grace, and denies that man's purely natural endowments would have been any healthier before sin than they are now after it.

Further on he even grants that man could have been made in such a state of pure nature that he would have had a headlong bent toward vice and the drive of sensuality. And he insists that nothing absurd would follow if God refused a man so created the grace that heals these evils and that man needs to reach eternal blessedness.

source_text: XXIII. Caeterum negat ibidem Bellarminus, Hominem sic in puris naturalibus creatum, propterea futurum esse in diaboli potestate. Qua in re a sententia Ruardi Tapperi recedit. Is enim affirmat hominem posse a Deo creari sine Originali justitia. Et tunc non solum in eo locum habituras jam dictas infirmitates, difficultatem, & ignorantiam; sed etiam illum affligendum fore omnibus iis quae experimur malis, etiam damnatione, & daemonum vexatione. Nam, inquit, creari posset homo sine justitia Originali, & omnibus malis quae nunc experimur, affligeretur, morbis scilicet, damnatione, daemonum vexatione, & universis aliis, quae tamen in eo non essent supplicia & poenae sed cruciatus tantum, sicut sunt in bestiis. In explicatione secundi articuli facultatis Lovaniensis, pag. 72. ubi agit de peccato Originali.
english: In the same place, however, Bellarmine denies that a man so created in a purely natural state would for that reason be in the devil's power. Here he parts from Ruard Tapper.

Tapper holds that God can create man without original righteousness, and that such a man would then not only suffer the weaknesses already named, difficulty and ignorance, but would also be afflicted with every evil we experience, even damnation and harassment by demons.

"Man could be created without original righteousness," he says, "and be afflicted with all the evils we now experience: diseases, damnation, harassment by demons and all the rest. In him, though, they would not be punishments and penalties, only torments, as they are in the beasts." So Tapper writes in his explanation of the second article of the Louvain faculty, page 72, where he deals with original sin.

source_text: XXIV. Quod spectat autem Protestantes, & qui inter eos speciali nomine Reformati dicuntur, communi consensu illi quoque docent Deum creavisse hominem in Justitia & Sanctitate vera: juxta illud Ecclesiastae, Deus fecit hominem rectum. Nec enim rectitudo ista alia in re consistere potest, quam in conformitate cum voluntate & lege divina, in qua hominis justitia consistit. Quo etiam Paulum respicere putant, dum fideles hortatur, ut induant novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est in justitia & sanctitate veritatis. Ubi manifestum est illum alludere ad primam creationem, in qua homo creatus dicitur ad Dei imaginem & similitudinem; ad quam ex ejus mente, pertinet sanctitas & justitia illa, quam Christus in fidelibus spiritu suo operatur.
english: The Protestants, and especially those among them called the Reformed, likewise teach by common consent that God created man in true righteousness and holiness, as the Preacher says: "God made man upright." That uprightness can consist in nothing else than conformity with God's will and law, which is what man's righteousness consists in.

They think Paul has the same thing in view when he urges believers to "put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness." He is plainly alluding there to the first creation, in which man is said to have been made in God's image and likeness. In Paul's mind that image includes the holiness and righteousness that Christ works in believers by his Spirit.

source_text: XXV. Caeterum sanctitatem & justitiam illam in qua primus homo a Deo conditus est, non in eo solum constituunt, quod Deum creatorem suum, uti par erat, agnoscebat, & puro ac syncero amore ei adhaerebat; sed in eo quoque quod omnes ejus facultates sic bene constitutae & ordinatae erant, ut inferiores superioribus, superiores vero Deo sine difficultate & repugnantia parerent: nec in eo ulla esset aut ad malum proclivitas, aut ad bene agendum difficultas & renitentia: qualis est illa quae jam in omnibus & singulis hominibus reperitur. Proindeque ex eorum sententia, in homine recens condito nihil inordinatum, nihil immoderatum fuit. Nec in eo locum habuit ulla ἀταξία, vel pugna facultatum illius inter se: sed omnes ejus facultates summa cum εὐταξίᾳ inter se concordes atque ordinatae, eundem finem, videlicet illum ad quem a Deo naturae authore creatus fuit, conspirabant.
english: They do not place the holiness and righteousness in which God made the first man only in his acknowledging God as his creator, as was fitting, and clinging to him with pure and sincere love. They place it also in the good constitution and order of all his faculties: the lower obeyed the higher and the higher obeyed God without difficulty or resistance, and he had no leaning to evil and no difficulty or reluctance in doing good, such as is now found in every single human being.

So in their view nothing in newly created man was disordered and nothing was excessive. There was no disorder (ataxia) in him and no conflict among his faculties. All of them, in the most perfect good order (eutaxia), agreed with one another and worked together toward one and the same end, the end for which God, the author of nature, had created him.

source_text: XXVI. Porro justitiam istam primo homini ante lapsum naturalem fuisse, & dici debere contendunt. Non quidem quod fuerit pars essentiam naturae humanae constituens, aut quod ex humanae naturae principiis necessario fluxerit: sed quia fuit aliquid naturae concreatum, & ad dotes nativas humanae naturae nondum lapsae pertinens. Adeoque justitia illa Originalis, secundum eorum doctrinam, donum naturale fuit, non supernaturale. Et se habet respectu animae hominis integri, quomodo respectu corporis se habebat justa membrorum proportio & pulchritudo, vigor atque decor, quae in eo tum reperiebantur, quaeque naturalem quandam, non vero supernaturalem perfectionem hominis spectabant: licet non essent de essentia hominis, neque etiam ex naturae humanae principiis necessario fluerent.
english: They further maintain that this righteousness was natural to the first man before the fall and should be called natural. They do not mean that it was a part making up the essence of human nature, or that it flowed necessarily from the principles of human nature. They mean that it was created together with that nature and belonged to the native endowments of human nature before the fall. On their teaching, then, original righteousness was a natural gift, not a supernatural one.

It stood to the soul of unfallen man as the due proportion and beauty of the limbs, their strength and grace, then stood to his body. Those belonged to a natural, not a supernatural, perfection of man, even though they were not part of his essence and did not flow necessarily from the principles of human nature.

source_text: XXVII. Sed ut clarius & certius in hac quaestione Scholae Reformatae sententia percipiatur, operae pretium erit breviter hic referre, quomodo praecipui aliquot illius Doctores mentem suam hac de re explicent: maxime cum videri posset inter eos hic esse nonnulla diversitas. Primum igitur Tilenus Syntagmatis Theologici parte prima, Disputatione trigesima tertia, Thesi decima quarta asserit, justitiam illam recte dici naturalem, eo sensu quo naturalia & supernaturalia mutuo sibi opponuntur, & ab invicem distinguuntur. Thesi vero decima septima dicit tam naturalem primo parenti fuisse hanc justitiae originalis qualitatem, quam erat ipsa natura & forma substantialis per creationem accepta. Adeoque Thesi praecedenti affirmat qualitatem istam ex primigenia Dei in homine imagine confestim emicuisse, ut solent accidentia ex subjectis suis.
english: To make the Reformed school's view on this question clearer and surer, it will be worth setting out briefly how some of its leading teachers explain their meaning, all the more because there might seem to be some difference among them here.

Tilenus comes first. In the first part of his Syntagma of Theology, disputation 33, thesis 14, he says that original righteousness is rightly called natural in the sense in which natural and supernatural are set against each other and distinguished. In thesis 17 he says that this quality of original righteousness was as natural to our first parent as nature itself and the substantial form he received in creation. And in the thesis before that he says the quality shone out at once from God's original image in man, as accidents commonly do from their subjects.

source_text: XXVIII. Amesius in Bellarmino Enervato tomo quarto capite primo, explicans quomodo justitia Originalis primo homini naturalis fuerit, Nos non dicimus, inquit, justitiam illam fuisse vel essentialem partem naturae Physicae, aut Physico modo ex ejus principiis fluere, sed conditionem esse moralem naturae illi debitam, quae ad juste operandum fuit creata.
english: William Ames, in volume 4, chapter 1 of his Bellarmine Disarmed, explains how original righteousness was natural to the first man: "We do not say that this righteousness was an essential part of physical nature or flowed from its principles in a physical way. We say it was a moral condition owed to that nature, which was created to act righteously."

source_text: XXIX. Josue Placeus in Syntagmate Thesium Salmuriensium Disputatione de statu Adami ante lapsum, Thesi decima octava, dicit rectitudinem originalem primi hominis naturalibus donis annumerandam fuisse, quoniam nihil aliud fuit, quam congruentia cum lege naturae, & perfectio quae fuit simul cum natura creata, & quae per naturalem generationem propaganda erat, adeoque perfectio naturalis naturalibus hominis facultatibus respondens. Thesi vero vigesima sexta concedit justitiam Originalem fuisse quidem gratiam, hoc est, donum gratuitum ab eisdem tribus personis profectum, a quibus natura ipsa creata fuit: & gratiam non fuisse, quo sensu hoc nomen opponitur naturae, & significat effecta favoris divini quo Deus peccatores prosequitur in Christo.
english: Josué de la Place, in the Syntagma of Saumur Theses, disputation on the state of Adam before the fall, thesis 18, says that the first man's original rectitude should be counted among natural gifts. It was nothing other than agreement with the law of nature, a perfection created together with nature and meant to be handed on by natural generation, and so a natural perfection answering to man's natural faculties.

In thesis 26 he grants that original righteousness was indeed a grace, in the sense of a free gift coming from the same three persons who created nature itself. But it was not a grace in the sense in which the word is opposed to nature and means the effects of the divine favor with which God follows sinners in Christ.

source_text: XXX. Sic vero suam ea de re mentem exponit Petrus Molinaeus. Contendimus, inquit, Adamo ante lapsum naturale fuisse Deum cognoscere & amare. Nec in natura integra agnoscimus ullam proclivitatem ad rebellionem, quia nihil erat quod coerceretur, quamvis esset quod regeretur. Nec putamus puritatem Adami ante lapsum fuisse fraenum extrinsecus injectum, aut sessorem adhibitum, sed virtutem naturalem. Disputat. de statu Innocentiae. Thesi XXV. in Thesauro Thesium Sedanensium.
english: Pierre du Moulin explains his view on this as follows: "We maintain that before the fall it was natural for Adam to know and love God. In unfallen nature we recognize no leaning toward rebellion, for there was nothing that had to be held in check, though there was something that had to be governed. Nor do we think that Adam's purity before the fall was a bridle put on him from outside, or a rider set on his back, but a natural strength." (Disputation on the State of Innocence, thesis 25, in the Thesaurus of Sedan Theses.)

source_text: XXXI. Pareus autem in librum Bellarmini de Gratia primi hominis cap. 1. dicit supernaturale esse quod homini supra naturae principia, vel dotes nativas inest ad ejus perfectionem. Naturam autem distinguit in integram, qualis erat in statu creationis ante lapsum, & in corruptam, qualis est in statu peccati. Unde observat supernaturale duobus modis dici. Vel enim significat id quod est supra naturam integram, vel id quod est supra naturam corruptam. Jam vero concedit justitiam originalem supernaturalem fuisse posteriori modo, quia superabat naturam corruptam. Sed negat priori modo fuisse supernaturalem, quoniam videlicet, non fuit supra dotes & perfectiones nativas naturae integrae. Capite vero quinto dicit defendi posse justitiam Originis primo homini tanquam naturae bonum fuisse naturalem, non minus quam facultatem videndi, sentiendi, &c. Quoniam ex mente illuminata notitiae illustres de Deo & rebus divinis: ex voluntate & corde justo Sancto, ut ex limpidissimo fonte operationes justae Sanctae scaturiebant, non minus naturaliter, licet mediante libero arbitrio, quam visio ex oculo, &c. Sed addit non esse necesse hoc urgere, propterea quod Adamo naturale fuit, non tantum quicquid ejus naturam constituebat, vel ex principiis naturae constitutae per se fluebat: sed etiam quicquid principiis naturae ad ejus perfectionem per se adjacebat, & sine quo natura in suis principiis non erat primitus condita. Ad quem vocis naturalis sensum potissimum spectare Theologos nostros affirmat, quum justitiam Originis primo homini fuisse naturalem contendunt. Unde colligit Bellarminum pervertere statum quaestionis, dum docet hic non quaeri, An justitia Originalis primo homini naturalis fuerit, prout naturale significat id quod inest a nativitate, quod utrinque conceditur, sed an fuerit naturalis, prout naturale distinguitur a supernaturali, & significat vel id quod naturam constituit, vel aptum est fluere ex principiis naturae.
english: Pareus, commenting on chapter 1 of Bellarmine's book On the Grace of the First Man, says that the supernatural is whatever is in man, for his perfection, above the principles of nature or his native endowments. He divides nature into unfallen nature, as it was at creation before the fall, and corrupt nature, as it is in the state of sin. So, he notes, "supernatural" is used in two ways: for what is above unfallen nature, or for what is above corrupt nature. He grants that original righteousness was supernatural in the second way, since it surpassed corrupt nature, but denies that it was supernatural in the first way, since it did not go beyond the native endowments and perfections of unfallen nature.

On chapter 5 he says it can be defended that original righteousness was natural to the first man as a good of his nature, no less than the power of seeing or sensing. For bright knowledge of God and divine things came from his enlightened mind, and righteous and holy acts welled up from his righteous and holy will and heart as from a perfectly clear spring, no less naturally, though through free choice, than sight comes from the eye.

But he adds that there is no need to press this point. What was natural to Adam was not only whatever made up his nature or flowed of itself from the principles of that nature, but also whatever of itself accompanied the principles of nature for its perfection, and without which nature was not first made in its principles. That, he says, is the sense of "natural" our theologians chiefly have in mind when they maintain that original righteousness was natural to the first man.

From this he concludes that Bellarmine twists the point at issue when he says the question here is not whether original righteousness was natural to the first man in the sense of what is there from birth, which both sides grant, but whether it was natural as natural is distinguished from supernatural, meaning either what makes up nature or what is fitted to flow from nature's principles.

source_text: XXXII. Denique Ramburtius in Sedanensium Thesium Syntagmate Disputatione de imagine Dei in homine, & justitia Originali. Thesi vigesima septima sic de hac quaestione sententiam suam pronunciat, Nos statuimus justitiam Originalem complecti totam hominis integritatem & sanctitatem, eamque homini fuisse naturalem: ita ut in Adae natura, simul atque extitit, insitum fuerit diligere Deum, eique obtemperare, hocque dono excelluisse hominem statim atque conditus est. Quod ita non volumus accipi ac si ex naturae viribus profluxerit haec sanctitas; sed quod nativa fuerit homini haec integritas: ita ut in eo per naturam, ut a Deo conditus est, & in hoc statu substitit, nulli fuerint motus inordinati: quemadmodum naturalem dicimus esse aliquam cognitionem Dei, quatenus nihil est tam naturale, quam quod ita naturae insidet, ut sine ejus, ut sic dicam, ejuratione non possit amoveri. Haec igitur justitia fulsit in Adamo simul ac exortus est, nihilque huic justitiae tepugnans expertus est.
english: Finally Abraham Rambour, in the Syntagma of Sedan Theses, disputation on the image of God in man and original righteousness, thesis 27, gives his view on the question in these words: "We hold that original righteousness includes the whole integrity and holiness of man, and that it was natural to him. Loving God and obeying him were planted in Adam's nature from the moment it existed, and man excelled in this gift from the moment he was made.

"We do not want this to be taken as though this holiness flowed from the powers of nature, but in the sense that this integrity was native to man, so that in him, by nature as God made him and while he stood in that state, there were no disordered movements. In the same way we call some knowledge of God natural, since nothing is so natural as what is so lodged in nature that it cannot be removed without, so to speak, nature's renouncing it on oath. This righteousness, then, shone in Adam as soon as he came into being, and he felt nothing in himself that resisted it."

source_text: XXXIII. Ex his autem apparet multos ex Reformatis manifeste docere justitiam Originalem primo homini naturalem fuisse, quoniam erat perfectio ordinis naturalis, creaturae rationali peccato nondum corruptae debita, ut quae ex naturae humanae, quae pura & innocens adhuc supponitur, facultatibus veluti emicat: non secus ac sanitas & bona valetudo ex corpore secundum naturam recte se habente. Alios vero, ut Pareum in primis, videri justitiam illam eo tantum nomine primo homini naturalem dicere, quod esset perfectio quaedam primo homini concreata, & quae ad ejus nativas & Originales dotes pertinebat. Ac quum supernaturalem illam fuisse negant, non aliud sibi velle, quam illam non fuisse aliquid primigeniis & nativis dotibus hominis superadditum.
english: From this it is plain that many of the Reformed openly teach that original righteousness was natural to the first man because it was a perfection of the natural order, owed to a rational creature not yet corrupted by sin, shining out, as it were, from the faculties of human nature, still taken to be pure and innocent, just as health and soundness shine out from a body that is in the condition nature intends.

Others, Pareus above all, seem to call that righteousness natural to the first man only because it was a perfection created together with him and belonged to his native, original endowments. When they deny it was supernatural, they mean only that it was not something added on top of man's first, native endowments.

source_text: XXXIV. Utcunque tamen de eo sit, & quacunque tandem ratione dicatur Originalis justitia primo homini fuisse naturalis, communis videtur esse Reformatorum sententia, omnino bonitati & sapientiae divinae repugnare, ut Deus hominem condat absque justitia Originali, & talem qui Deum, ut par est, non agnoscat & amet, & ad malum sit pronus atque proclivis, & in quo sensus atque appetitus rationi repugnant, & sint legi divinae rebelles. Nec enim existimant ejusmodi erga Deum amoris privationem, & praecipitem ad malum & vitia inclinationem, ac rebellionem sensus & appetitus adversus mentem, & legem divinam in creatura rationali posse peccato & culpa carere. Adeoque absurdum & creatori injurium ducunt, si dicatur ejusmodi inferiorum animae facultatum rebellionem, & quae inde sequitur totius hominis ad malum pronitatem, & repugnantiam ad bonum aliquid esse consequens hominis compositionem ex anima rationali & corpore organico, quodque necessario, & secundum ipsam rerum naturam inde resultat, nisi Deus aliquid supra naturam addat, quod subjiciat rationem Deo, & partem inferiorem animae rationi subdat.
english: However that may be, and on whatever ground original righteousness is said to have been natural to the first man, the common Reformed view seems to be that it is wholly at odds with God's goodness and wisdom for him to make man without original righteousness: a man who does not know and love God as he should, who leans and inclines toward evil, and in whom sense and appetite resist reason and rebel against God's law.

They do not believe that in a rational creature such a lack of love for God, such a headlong bent to evil and vice, and such a rebellion of sense and appetite against the mind and God's law, can be free of sin and guilt.

So they think it absurd, and an insult to the Creator, to say that this rebellion of the soul's lower faculties, with the proneness of the whole man to evil and his resistance to good that follow from it, is a consequence of man's being made of a rational soul and an organic body, something that results from that make-up necessarily and by the very nature of things unless God adds something above nature to subject reason to God and the lower part of the soul to reason.

source_text: XXXV. Ac proinde plane fictitium & impossibilem censent statum illum hominis in puris naturalibus, cujus saepe in Schola Romana mentio fit; in quo supponitur homo peccato non corruptus, & tamen justitia & sanctitate vacuus, Deoque non adhaerens puro & casto amore, sed propria concupiscentia ad inferiora tractus, ignorans quae ad veram beatitudinem necessaria sunt, ad bonum perficiendum infirmus & impotens, & ad vitia praecipiti inclinatione proclivis, sicut colligere est ex Doctorum Reformatorum, qui supra citati sunt, & plurimorum aliorum dissertationibus, dum de justitia Originali adversus Bellarminum, aliosque Doctores Scholae Romanae disputant.
english: They therefore regard as plainly fictitious and impossible the state of man "in a purely natural condition" that the Roman school so often speaks of. In it man is supposed to be uncorrupted by sin and yet empty of righteousness and holiness: not clinging to God with a pure and chaste love but dragged toward lower things by his own concupiscence, ignorant of what true blessedness requires, weak and unable to do good, and inclined headlong toward vice.

This can be gathered from the treatises of the Reformed teachers cited above, and of many others, where they argue about original righteousness against Bellarmine and other teachers of the Roman school.

source_text: XXXVI. Pareus tamen asserere non audet, non potuisse naturam humanam absque Originali justitia creari. Nec dicimus, inquit, naturam humanam non potuisse a Deo sine Originali justitia creari. Nos enim terminum divinae ponemus potentiae? saltem dicimus Deum, cum hominem integrum conderet, non potuisse seipsum negare; hominem integrum sine integritate condere. In libr. 1. Bellarm. de Grat. Primi hominis cap. 6. Responsione ad rationem quartam.
english: Pareus, however, does not venture to assert that human nature could not have been created without original righteousness. "We do not say," he writes, "that God could not have created human nature without original righteousness. Are we to put a boundary to God's power? What we do say is that when God made man whole, he could not deny himself by making a whole man without wholeness." (On Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, book 1, chapter 6, reply to the fourth argument.)

source_text: XXXVII. Porro quamvis pertendant Doctores Reformati justitiam Originalem primo homini fuisse naturalem, affirmare tamen nolunt, saltem eorum complures, primum hominem caruisse omni gratia supernaturali, & non aliis quam naturalibus donis a Deo fuisse ornatum. Illud praesertim videre est apud Petrum Molinaeum, supra citata disputatione de statu innocentiae, thesi 49. & 50. Non imus tamen inficias, inquit, quin in Adamo fuerint quaedam dona supernaturalia. Nam si aliquam cognitionem hauserat ex revelatione: aut si quid habuit ad quod humana natura quantumvis pura non potuit pervenire sine dono Dei peculiari & extraordinario, id sine dubio fuit supernaturale: nec id Adam perstans in integritate ad posteros propagasset. Praeterea quemadmodum non dubium est quin homo quantumvis perfecto corporis temperamento naturali, opus habeat auxilio supernaturali, & Dei ope continua, ad servandam hanc εὐκρασίαν: ita etsi Adami natura esset pura & sancta, opus tamen habebat jugi auxilio supernaturali ad conservandam istam puritatem. Cum etiam inanimata & irrationalia divino sustentur influxu.
english: Although the Reformed teachers maintain that original righteousness was natural to the first man, many of them at least will not say that he lacked all supernatural grace and that God adorned him with natural gifts only. This is especially clear in Pierre du Moulin, in the disputation on the state of innocence cited above, theses 49 and 50.

"We do not deny," he says, "that there were some supernatural gifts in Adam. If he drew any knowledge from revelation, or had anything that human nature, however pure, could not reach without a special and extraordinary gift of God, that was without doubt supernatural, and Adam would not have passed it on to his descendants even had he persevered in his integrity.

"Again, there is no doubt that a man, however perfect his body's natural balance, needs supernatural help and God's constant aid to keep that good balance (eukrasia). In the same way, though Adam's nature was pure and holy, it still needed continual supernatural help to keep that purity, since even lifeless and irrational things are upheld by God's inflowing power."

source_text: XXXVIII. Ramburtius similiter in Adamo agnoscit dona supernaturalia, thesi vigesima nona modo citatae disputationis. Neque propterea, inquit, dona supernaturalia ab Adamo removemus. Gratia enim Dei haec eadem dona naturalia exornabat, in dies attollebat: quemadmodum gratia non destruit naturam, sed eam dirigit, & altius quam quo per vires suas eniti potest erigit. Ideo primus homo non modo fuit eximia creatura, sed etiam filius Dei, assumptus ad cernendam haereditatem caelestem, id est, non tantum habuit per naturam rationem servi fidelis, Domini voluntatem probe intelligentis, eamque perfecte exequentis, sed etiam per gratiam dignitatem filii paternam benedictionem & haereditatem sperantis.
english: Rambour likewise recognizes supernatural gifts in Adam, in thesis 29 of the disputation just cited: "This does not mean that we take supernatural gifts away from Adam. God's grace adorned these same natural gifts and lifted them higher day by day, just as grace does not destroy nature but directs it and raises it higher than it can climb by its own strength.

"So the first man was not only an outstanding creature but also a son of God, adopted to enter into the heavenly inheritance. By nature he had the standing of a faithful servant who understood his Lord's will well and carried it out perfectly; by grace he also had the dignity of a son who hoped for his Father's blessing and inheritance."

source_text: XXXIX. Quibus similia apud Tilenum legere est. Criminose, inquit, & calumniose Pelagianorum sententiam nobis affingunt Pontificii, quasi nulla supernaturalia dona in primo homine fuisse contendamus, cum Theologicas virtutes ipsi tribuamus διαρρήδην. De justitia Originali thesi trigesima octava. Paulo ante vero distinctius explicans qua in re consisteret gratia Adamo collata, Ut a natura, inquit, id habebat voluntas Adami, ut posset juste & sancte operari, sic ut reapse operaretur, Deumque super omnia amaret, efficaciter movebatur a gratia. At quemadmodum vitis non propterea caret vi naturali ad proferendum vinum, quod externis illi opus est auxiliis, puta sole, pluvia & cultura, ut actu proferat, sic & in Adamo non ideo naturalis non fuit voluntatis rectitudo, & affectuum εὐταξία, licet in actu secundo gratiae moventis auxilio exercitaretur & adjuvaretur.
english: Similar things can be read in Tilenus: "The papists wickedly and slanderously pin the Pelagians' view on us, as though we held there were no supernatural gifts in the first man, when we expressly ascribe the theological virtues to him." (On Original Righteousness, thesis 38.)

A little earlier, explaining more precisely what the grace given to Adam consisted in, he says: "Adam's will had from nature the power to act righteously and holily; that it actually did so, and loved God above all things, came from its being moved effectively by grace.

"But a vine is not without a natural power to bear wine just because it needs outside help, such as sun, rain and tending, to bear it in fact. In the same way the uprightness of Adam's will and the good order (eutaxia) of his affections were still natural, even though in their actual exercise they were set to work and helped by moving grace."

source_text: XL. Proinde Doctor ille ad gratiam supernaturalem in primo homine refert, tum auxilium actuale quo excitabatur ad bene agendum, tum virtutes Theologicas fidem, spem, & charitatem quibus ornatus erat. Sed difficile capi potest quomodo virtutes istae in Adamo fuerint dona supernaturalia, & tamen rectitudo, seu justitia Originalis ipsi naturalis erat, aut quae possit esse justitia & Rectitudo Deo grata & accepta sine fide, spe, & charitate. Ut & in iis quae ante ex Ramburtio retulimus, non satis inter se concordare videntur quae simul affirmat doctissimus ille vir, nempe primi hominis justitiam & sanctitatem naturalem fuisse non supernaturalem, & tamen eam ex viribus naturae non profluxisse. Quomodo enim potest non esse supernaturale quod ex naturae viribus non profluit? Nisi dicamus eum cum Pareo supernaturale vocare quod adventitium est, & ad nativas dotes superadditur. Originalem vero justitiam eo solum nomine naturalem vocari, quod a prima Origine fuerit homini insita, & ipsi concreata, & sic ad nativas ejus dotes pertinuerit; quomodo ipse se videtur explicare. Quanquam non satis quadrat quod subjungit, justitiam primi hominis illi fuisse naturalem, sicut naturalis nobis est aliqua Dei cognitio. Nam cognitio illa Dei quam naturalem vocat, non superat naturae vires.
english: So Tilenus counts as supernatural grace in the first man both the actual help by which he was stirred to do good and the theological virtues, faith, hope and love, with which he was adorned. But it is hard to see how those virtues could have been supernatural gifts in Adam while his uprightness, or original righteousness, was natural to him. Or what righteousness and uprightness could please God and be accepted by him without faith, hope and love?

In the same way, in what we quoted earlier from Rambour, the things that very learned man asserts together do not seem to fit well: that the first man's righteousness and holiness was natural and not supernatural, and yet that it did not flow from the powers of nature. How can something not be supernatural if it does not flow from nature's powers?

Unless, that is, we say that he, like Pareus, calls supernatural whatever is acquired and added on top of native endowments, and calls original righteousness natural only because it was planted in man from his first origin, created together with him, and so belonged to his native endowments. That seems to be how he explains himself. Even so, what he adds does not quite square: that the first man's righteousness was natural to him as some knowledge of God is natural to us. The knowledge of God he calls natural does not go beyond nature's powers.

source_text: XLI. Ex iis autem quae hactenus exposita fuerunt, planum est Scholam Romanam, & Scholam Reformatam in eo consentire, quod primus homo ante lapsum praeditus fuerit vera justitia & sanctitate, per quam & Deum mente sicuti decet agnoscebat, & voluntate diligebat, nihilque habebat in se inordinatum, & quod legi ac voluntati divinae repugnaret, quodque se ultro rectae rationi non submitteret.
english: From what has been set out so far it is clear that the Roman and Reformed schools agree on this: before the fall the first man had true righteousness and holiness. Through it he knew God with his mind as he ought and loved him with his will, and he had nothing disordered in him, nothing at odds with God's law and will, nothing that would not freely submit to right reason.

source_text: XLII. Inde quoque manifestum est, Scholae Romanae Theologos, plerosque saltem, cum Reformatis docere primum hominem fuisse in justitia illa & sanctitate creatum; adeoque primum hominem nunquam ea caruisse, sed eam illi a prima Origine fuisse insitam.
english: It is also clear from this that most theologians of the Roman school, at least, teach with the Reformed that the first man was created in that righteousness and holiness. He was therefore never without it; it was planted in him from his first origin.

source_text: XLIII. Proindeque quod illinc manifeste sequitur, plerique Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae cum Protestantibus agnoscunt justitiam Originalem primo homini naturalem fuisse, quatenus naturale significat idem quod nativum, & opponitur ei quod est adventitium & superadditum.
english: It plainly follows that most teachers of the Roman Church grant, with the Protestants, that original righteousness was natural to the first man in the sense in which "natural" means the same as "native" and is opposed to what is acquired and added on top.

source_text: XLIV. Imo patet ex iis quae ante retulimus, in Ecclesia Romana non deesse, qui cum plerisque Reformatis doceant justitiam Originalem pertinuisse ad dona naturae, non gratiae, prout naturae opponitur: adeoque primo homini naturalem fuisse, quatenus naturale opponitur supernaturali.
english: In fact, what we reported earlier shows that the Roman Church has its own teachers who side with most of the Reformed here. They hold that original righteousness was one of nature's gifts, not one of grace's, taking grace as the opposite of nature. On their view it was natural to the first man even in the sense that stands against "supernatural".

source_text: XLV. Praeterea, ut ex dictis colligere est, in Ecclesia Romana non pauci Reformatis concedunt justitiam Originalem, qualiscunque tandem dicenda sit, seu naturalis, seu supernaturalis, fuisse perfectionem ita homini innocenti debitam, ut salva sapientia & bonitate divina, non potuerit absque illa creari: adeoque statum hominis in puris naturalibus, qualem describit Scholae Romanae vulgus, & in quo supponitur homo non peccator, & tamen justitia vacuus, & in vitia pronus, ac concupiscentia rationi rectae repugnanti laborans, esse aliquid mere fictitium; & quod bonitas, justitia, & sapientia divina in rerum natura unquam dari prohibent.
english: Again, as can be gathered from what has been said, a good many in the Roman Church grant the Reformed that original righteousness, whatever it should finally be called, natural or supernatural, was a perfection so owed to innocent man that God could not have created him without it without compromising his wisdom and goodness.

They grant too that the state of man in a purely natural condition, as the ordinary run of the Roman school describes it, in which man is supposed to be no sinner and yet empty of righteousness, prone to vice and struggling with a concupiscence that fights right reason, is a mere fiction, something God's goodness, justice and wisdom forbid ever to exist in reality.

source_text: XLVI. Vicissim vero Protestantes Doctoribus Scholae Romanae concedunt justitiam Originalem non fuisse primo homini naturalem, quatenus naturale significat, id quod naturam constituit, aut quod necessario, sive modo physico, fluit ex humanae naturae principiis. Ac praeterea multi Scholae Reformatae Doctores non negant primum hominem habuisse dona quaedam supernaturalia: & gratiam quandam homini, etiam innocenti, necessariam fuisse, ut recte & secundum justitiam operaretur. Quin eorum nonnulli justitiam Originalem ex naturae viribus non fluxisse fatentur.
english: The Protestants, for their part, grant the teachers of the Roman school that original righteousness was not natural to the first man in the sense of what makes up nature, or of what flows necessarily, that is physically, from the principles of human nature.

Many teachers of the Reformed school also do not deny that the first man had some supernatural gifts, and that even innocent man needed some grace in order to act rightly and righteously. Some of them even admit that original righteousness did not flow from the powers of nature.

source_text: XLVII. Verum hic controversia est inter Scholam Romanam, paucissimis exceptis, & inter Scholam Reformatam, Num justitia Originalis primo homini naturalis fuerit, vel supernaturalis. Naturalem fuisse non supernaturalem communi consensu affirmant Scholae Reformatae Doctores; contra vero Scholae Romanae Theologi plerique omnes pertendunt illam fuisse non naturalem, sed supernaturalem. Quae quidem controversia respectu quorundam Theologorum realis, respectu vero aliorum verbalis esse videtur. Realis est respectu eorum qui sentiunt justitiam Originalem fuisse perfectionem ordinis naturalis, naturalibus hominis facultatibus respondentem, & quae non ad gratiam sed ad naturam pertinebat. Reapse enim contrarium significare volunt Scholae Romanae Theologi, quum asserunt justitiam illam fuisse supernaturalem. Sed eadem controversia verbalis est respectu aliorum, qui docent justitiam istam non aliter primo homini fuisse naturalem, quam quia erat illi concreata, & inter dotes ejus nativas numerari debet. Ac quum eandem justitiam negant fuisse supernaturalem, nihil aliud significare volunt, quam eam non fuisse homini supra primigenias dotes superadditam. Quod concedunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, saltem eorum quamplurimi.
english: The real dispute here, between the Roman school (with very few exceptions) and the Reformed school, is whether original righteousness was natural or supernatural to the first man. The Reformed teachers say by common consent that it was natural and not supernatural; almost all the Roman theologians, on the other hand, insist that it was supernatural and not natural.

With some theologians this dispute seems to be about substance, with others only about words. It is a dispute of substance with those who hold that original righteousness was a perfection of the natural order, answering to man's natural faculties and belonging to nature rather than to grace. When the Roman theologians call that righteousness supernatural, they really do mean the opposite.

With the others it is a dispute about words. They teach that original righteousness was natural to the first man only because it was created with him and should be counted among his native endowments, and when they deny that it was supernatural they mean only that it was not added to man over and above his first endowments. That the Roman teachers grant, or a great many of them do.

source_text: XLVIII. Praeterea vero quaestio est inter Scholam Reformatam & plurimos Scholae Romanae Doctores, Annon sapientiae & bonitati divinae repugnet hominem creari absque justitia Originali; & an inter status hominis possibiles numerari debeat status ille quem Schola Romana vocat purae naturae: In quo non sit homo peccato corruptus, & tamen vera justitia careat, multaque ignorantia & infirmitate laboret, & ad malum trahatur propria concupiscentia, & appetitu adversus rationem rebellante, non secus ac res se habet in statu naturae corruptae. Quod affirmat vulgus Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae, Schola vero Reformata communi consensu negat, uno forte vel altero excepto.
english: There is a further question between the Reformed school and a great many Roman teachers: whether it is not contrary to God's wisdom and goodness for man to be created without original righteousness, and whether the state the Roman school calls "pure nature" should be counted among man's possible states.

In that state man would not be corrupted by sin, yet would lack true righteousness, would struggle with much ignorance and weakness, and would be drawn toward evil by his own concupiscence and by an appetite rebelling against reason, just as things are in the state of corrupt nature. The ordinary run of Roman teachers says yes; the Reformed school, with perhaps one or two exceptions, says no by common consent.

source_text: XLIX. Et certe nisi ita statuamus, gravissima sequentur absurda. Primo enim inde sequetur concupiscentiam illam, per quam caro pugnat adversus spiritum, & quam Scholae Romanae Doctores, etiam post remissum peccatum Originale, concedunt habere rationem vitii, & mali cujusdam moralis, quod Deo displicens & odiosum est, quamque Joannes negat esse a Patre, sequetur, inquam, inde concupiscentiam illam potuisse habere Deum ipsum authorem; qui scilicet, ex hac hypothesi, hominem cum illa creare potuerit. Nec vim argumenti tollit quod Bellarminus Respondet, concupiscentiam istam ex materia fuisse emersuram, praeter Dei intentionem: Ut rubiginem ex gladio, cujus propterea faber ferrarius author non est. Nam faber ferrarius non fecit ferri materiam unde rubigo exoritur, sicut Deus corporis nostri materiam creavit. Et tamen, citra fabri culpam, non potest inesse rubigo gladio ex manibus illius prodeunti.
english: Indeed, unless we hold this, the gravest absurdities follow. First, it will follow that God himself could be the author of the concupiscence by which the flesh fights against the spirit, since on this hypothesis he could have created man with it. Yet the Roman teachers grant that this concupiscence, even after original sin has been forgiven, has the character of a vice and of a moral evil that God finds displeasing and hateful, and John denies that it comes from the Father.

Bellarmine's reply does not remove the force of this argument. He says that concupiscence would have arisen from matter apart from God's intention, as rust arises on a sword, and the smith is not therefore its author. But the smith did not make the iron from which the rust comes, whereas God did create the matter of our bodies. And even so, rust cannot be on a sword fresh from the smith's hands unless the smith is at fault.

source_text: L. Posito enim quod Deus hominem aliquem creet cum eadem ignorantia, proclivitate ad malum, & repugnantia ad bonum, cum qua jam ex Adamo nascimur; nec ulla gratia supernaturali illum juvare velit, quod fieri posse censent communiter Scholastici, homo ille nec Deum diliget, nec actus & affectus suos ad normam rectae rationis componet, sed libidini suae in omnibus indulgebit, & in diversa flagitia, prout se dabit occasio necessario ruet; ut faceret homo ex Adamo natus, si omni gratiae divinae auxilio destitueretur. Ac proinde sic Deus erit author peccati; ut qui creaverit hominem, qui nulla sua culpa, sed quali illum Deo, formare visum fuit, peccatum vitare non potest, ac quodam naturae vitio & impetu in varia scelera sese praecipitem eat, nec creatorem suum, sicuti par est, diligere valet. Vel dicendum est dari posse creaturam rationalem, quae Deum agnoscere & amare non tenebitur, quaeque poterit se omni immunditia polluere, & irae luxuriae ac gulae indulgere, stuprisque & caedibus in sui similes grassari, & reliqua patrari quae lex naturae & aeterna vetat, nec tamen propterea ullius criminis & peccati rea fiet. Quorum utrumque est vehementer absurdum; & manifestam quandam impietatem involvit.
english: Suppose God created a man with the same ignorance, the same leaning toward evil and resistance to good with which we are now born of Adam, and chose not to help him with any supernatural grace, as the scholastics commonly think could happen. That man would not love God or shape his acts and affections by the rule of right reason. He would give way to his desires in everything and would inevitably plunge into one crime after another as occasion arose, just as a child of Adam would do if he were left without any help from God's grace.

God would then be the author of sin, since he would have created a man who, through no fault of his own but simply because God chose to make him so, cannot avoid sin, rushes headlong into crimes of every kind by a flaw and drive in his nature, and cannot love his Creator as he ought.

Otherwise we would have to say there could be a rational creature not bound to know and love God, one that could defile itself with every impurity, give way to anger, excess and gluttony, assault its fellows with rape and murder, and do everything else the natural and eternal law forbids, and still not be guilty of any crime or sin. Both conclusions are utterly absurd and plainly involve impiety.

source_text: LI. Hoc autem semel concesso, fieri non posse ut homo a Deo creetur absque justitia & sanctitate, tanti momenti non videtur altera illa quaestio. An Justitia & Sanctitas illa in qua Deus primum hominem condidit, & sine qua creari a Deo non potuit, pertineat ad naturae, vel ad gratiae dotes, & naturalis dicenda sit, vel supernaturalis: Modo, quod omnes concedunt, statuamus illam esse gratuitum Dei donum, quod nullis creaturae meritis debebatur.
english: Once it is granted that God cannot create man without righteousness and holiness, the other question does not seem so important: whether the righteousness and holiness in which God made the first man, and without which God could not have created him, belongs to the endowments of nature or of grace, and should be called natural or supernatural. That holds provided we affirm, as everyone grants, that it is God's free gift, owed to no merit of the creature.

source_text: LII. Ratio tamen exigere videtur, ut dicamus illam ad naturae dotes pertinuisse, & naturalem potius fuisse quam supernaturalem. Etenim naturale non supernaturale est, id quod ad naturae rectam constitutionem pertinet, & sine quo natura nec sana est, nec recte constituta. Jam vero natura humana absque Sanctitate & Justitia illa, quae homini integro inerat, non sana, sed aegra est, nec potest dici recte constituta; si quidem facultatum inferiorum adversus rationem rebellio, & pronitas totius hominis ad rebellandum Deo, naturae rationalis morbus est & vitium quoddam.
english: Still, reason seems to require us to say that it belonged to the endowments of nature and was natural rather than supernatural. What belongs to the right constitution of a nature, without which that nature is neither healthy nor rightly formed, is natural, not supernatural.

Human nature without the holiness and righteousness that unfallen man had is not healthy but sick, and cannot be called rightly formed, if indeed the rebellion of the lower faculties against reason and the whole man's tendency to rebel against God are a disease and a defect of rational nature.

source_text: LIII. Praeterea creaturae rationali non corruptae naturale est id sine quo naturalem suum finem assequi nequit. Sed finis creaturae rationalis est, ut Deum agnoscat, amet atque colat. Ad hoc fuit enim a Deo condita. Hunc finem autem assequi non potest, si absque justitia & sanctitate creetur; Et si consideretur ut destituta donis illis quae per Adami peccatum amisimus.
english: Further, what an uncorrupted rational creature needs in order to reach its natural end is natural to it. The end of a rational creature is to know, love and worship God, for that is what God made it for.
It cannot reach that end if it is created without righteousness and holiness, that is, if it is thought of as stripped of the gifts we lost through Adam's sin.

source_text: LIV. Nec etiam est ulla naturalis facultas cui sua perfectio naturalis non respondeat. Morales autem facultates, ratione quarum homo est virtutis & vitii capax, homini naturales sunt, non minus quam caeterae. Qua in re autem earum naturalis perfectio consistere potest, nisi in ipsa justitia & sanctitate, de qua jam quaestio est?
english: Again, there is no natural faculty without a natural perfection that belongs to it. Man's moral faculties, which make him capable of virtue and vice, are as natural to him as his other faculties. What can their natural perfection be, if not the very righteousness and holiness now in question?

source_text: LV. Adde quod ad naturae dotes in creatura rationali non corrupta sed pura pertinet, ut conformis sit legi naturae, & ad illius regulas se componat. Ac proinde quicquid sine quo non potest naturae legi sese conformare, & omnes motus suos illi subdere, dotes & ordinem naturae non excedit. Ad legem autem naturae se componere non potest, homo destitutus omni justitia & sanctitate, & infirmitatibus illis quibuscum hodie nascimur, obnoxius. Adeoque sanctitas & justitia illa, per quam tolluntur tales infirmitates, ad naturae non corruptae dona spectare censenda est.
english: Add that it belongs to the endowments of nature in a rational creature that is not corrupt but pure to conform to the law of nature and shape itself by its rules. So whatever it needs in order to conform to the law of nature and bring all its impulses under it does not go beyond the endowments and order of nature.

But a man without any righteousness or holiness, and subject to the weaknesses we are born with today, cannot shape himself by the law of nature. So the holiness and righteousness that remove such weaknesses must be counted among the gifts of uncorrupted nature.

source_text: LVI. Unde videtur quoque cum ratione non satis congruere quod ex Reformatis nonnulli supra citati dicunt, licet justitia & sanctitas illa in qua primus homo creatus est, fuerit ei naturalis, illum tamen eguisse auxilio quodam supernaturali, quo ad bene agendum moveretur & excitaretur. Quanquam enim certum sit sine jugi Dei auxilio nihil boni unquam hominem agere, non tantum in rebus spiritualibus, sed ne quidem in rebus civilibus & humanis: adeoque ante lapsum ipsum opus fuisse homini perpetuo auxilio Dei, in quo vivimus, movemur, & sumus: Attamen non necesse est ut auxilium istud fuerit Ordinis supernaturalis; sed potuit ad hoc sufficere auxilium quod non superaret ordinem naturae primitus a Deo institutae. Nam auxilium requisitum ad hoc ut creatura quaeque nondum corrupta atque vitiata, naturae suae conformiter agat, & ad finem suum naturalem tendat, ad naturae ordinem pertinere existimandum est.
english: So it also seems not quite reasonable for some of the Reformed cited above to say that, although the righteousness and holiness in which the first man was created were natural to him, he still needed a supernatural help to move and stir him to do good.

It is certain that without God's constant help man never does any good, not only in spiritual matters but not even in civil and human ones, so that even before the fall man needed the continual help of God, in whom we live and move and have our being. But that help did not have to be of the supernatural order. Help that did not go beyond the order of nature as God first established it could have been enough. The help a creature not yet corrupted and spoiled needs in order to act in keeping with its nature and tend toward its natural end should be reckoned as belonging to the order of nature.

source_text: LVII. Verum inde non sequitur falsum esse quod diserte docent Reformati complures, nimirum in primo homine fuisse dona quaedam supernaturalia. Nam potuit Deus ad naturae primigeniae dotes, & auxilia ei necessaria, supra naturam quod libuit addere; sed quid illud & quantum fuerit, non audemus, scriptura tacente, definire. Illud tamen ex scriptura certum, in primo homine fuisse notitiam quandam supernaturalem: quandoquidem Deus illi supra naturam sese revelavit, & de voluntate sua expresso verbo illum edocuit.
english: It does not follow, however, that what many of the Reformed explicitly teach is false, namely that the first man had some supernatural gifts. God could have added to the endowments of man's first nature, and to the help it needed, whatever he pleased above nature. But what that was and how much, we do not venture to define, since Scripture is silent.
One thing Scripture does make certain: the first man had a certain supernatural knowledge, since God revealed himself to him beyond nature and taught him his will in express words.

source_text: LVIII. Neque ex eo quod homo constat corpore terreno & anima spirituali, sequitur in eo naturalem esse pugnam sensus & appetitus adversus rationem: adeoque talem pugnam atque rebellionem non posse tolli, nisi per donum supernaturale. Nam naturalis quidem est homini duplex inclinatio, una erga bonum terrenum, quatenus corporeus est, altera vero erga bonum spirituale, quatenus praeditus est anima intelligente: sed quemadmodum anima suo corpore longe praestantior est, ita quoque naturae recte constitutae convenit, ut corporis motus & inclinationes animae Imperiis & jussibus subjiciantur, & sic appetitus rationi pareat. Quum vero res aliter se habet, in eo apparet quaedam naturae deordinatio.
english: It does not follow, from man's being made of an earthly body and a spiritual soul, that the conflict of sense and appetite with reason is natural in him, or that such conflict and rebellion can only be removed by a supernatural gift.

Man does naturally have two inclinations, one toward earthly good because he has a body, the other toward spiritual good because he has an intelligent soul. But as the soul far surpasses its body, so a rightly formed nature requires that the body's impulses and inclinations be subject to the soul's commands, and so that appetite obey reason. Where it is otherwise, nature is plainly out of order.

source_text: LIX. Nec posito quod rectitudo homini concreata ipsa naturalis fuerit, non supernaturalis, ita difficile est, ut Bellarminus existimat, ostendere qua ratione corruptio illa quae jam nobis inest, & per quam ratio cogitur affectibus subesse, naturam humanam invasit. Vitium enim illud ortum habuit a parte animi superiore, quum a Deo discedens, ferri coepit in objectum appetitus sensitivi tanquam in finem suum. Nam inde secuta est facultatum moralium in homine ἀταξία. Siquidem primigenia earum rectitudo in eo consistebat quod ad Deum tanquam finem summum omnes illarum motus & affectus, ex mentis & rationis imperio, dirigebantur. A quo fine ratio deviare non potest, & bona terrena illi substituere, quin sensui & appetitui, quorum jam objectum pro fine summo est, turpiter, & contra propriam naturam servire cogatur.
english: Nor, granting that the rectitude created with man was itself natural and not supernatural, is it as hard as Bellarmine thinks to show how the corruption now in us, which forces reason to be subject to the passions, got into human nature.

That flaw began in the higher part of the soul, when it turned away from God and began to be carried toward the object of the sense appetite as though that were its end. The disorder (ataxia) of man's moral faculties followed from that. Their original rectitude lay in all their impulses and affections being directed, at the command of mind and reason, toward God as their highest end. Reason cannot turn aside from that end and put earthly goods in its place without being forced to serve sense and appetite, shamefully and against its own nature, since their object now stands for it in place of the highest end.
